final_answer:
Depth-First Search (DfS) and Breadth-First Search (BfS) are algorithms for traversing or searching tree or graph data structures. DfS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack (LIFO) to keep track of nodes. BfS, on the other hand, explores all neighbors at the current depth level before moving to nodes at the next depth level, using a queue (FIFO). 

DfS is useful for problems like finding connected components, detecting cycles, or solving puzzles with deep paths (e.g., mazes). BfS is optimal for finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph, as it explores nodes level by level. 

Choose DfS when memory is limited or the solution lies deep in the graph. Choose BfS when the shortest path is required or the graph is wide but shallow. Both have O(V + E) time complexity, but BfS uses more memory in wide graphs, while DfS risks stack overflow in deep trees.
